blocks.text:
Design a vending machine that sells snacks and drinks. A user inserts money, selects a product by its shelf code, and the machine dispenses the product along with the correct change. An operator can restock products and refill the coin float.

The system is a self contained physical machine driven by software. Its behaviour depends heavily on what has already happened: before money is inserted, selecting an item must do nothing; after money is inserted, the same button press starts a purchase. Modelling that changing behaviour cleanly is the core of this problem, and it is the classic showcase for the State design pattern.

  • Users: buyers who insert money and buy items, and operators who service the machine
  • Scope: one machine, in memory, with cash payments and an extensible payment abstraction
  • Goal: clean object oriented design that an interviewer can read top to bottom

The vending machine is not about snacks. It is about behaviour that changes with state.
These are the behaviours the machine must support for buyers and operators.

items: Accept money as coins and notes, one denomination at a time, and show a running balance
Let the user select a product by a shelf code such as A1
Validate the selection: the item exists, is in stock, the balance covers the price, and exact change is possible
Dispense the selected product
Return the correct change after a successful purchase
Allow the user to cancel at any point before dispensing and receive a full refund
Reject invalid actions with a clear reason instead of failing silently
Operator: restock shelves, refill the coin float, and collect accumulated cash

blocks.text: A single machine serves one buyer at a time, so raw throughput is not the concern. The design should still scale in catalogue size: hundreds of shelves must not slow selection down, which pushes us toward constant time lookups.
New payment methods, new denominations, new product types, and new machine modes must be added by writing new classes, not by editing existing, tested ones.
Each class should have one responsibility and be small enough to read in a minute. State specific behaviour must live in state classes, never in scattered if statements.
Every user action should complete in constant time. Selection is an O(1) map lookup and change making is bounded by the fixed number of denominations.
The check and decrement on a shelf must be atomic so two concurrent requests can never both win the last unit. Money movements must never be lost or double counted.
Before designing, confirm scope with the interviewer. Good questions here prevent building the wrong machine.

items: Payment methods: cash only, or should the design anticipate cards and wallets?
Change: must the machine guarantee exact change, and what happens when it cannot?
Cancellation: can the user cancel after selecting but before the item drops?
Inventory: is it one item per shelf code, or can a shelf hold mixed products?
Concurrency: is this a single keypad machine, or can multiple sessions run at once?
Persistence: is in memory state acceptable, or must transactions survive a restart?
Operator features: are restocking and cash collection in scope?

blocks.text: State the answers you assume out loud. In this design we assume cash first with a payment abstraction, exact change guaranteed before sale, cancel allowed until dispensing, one item type per shelf, a single session, in memory state, and operator features in scope.

items: All money is handled in cents as integers, never floating point, so totals are exact
Each shelf code maps to exactly one product with a fixed price
The machine holds a limited float of each denomination for change
One purchase happens at a time from a single keypad session
If exact change cannot be returned, the sale is refused before dispensing
State is in memory; persistence is discussed in the database section as an extension
Denominations are the standard currency set, so greedy change making is optimal

blocks.text: Constraints are not limitations, they are decisions that keep the design honest and the interview scoped.
blocks.content: Constraints are not limitations, they are decisions that keep the design honest and the interview scoped.

blocks.text: Underline the nouns in the requirements and the core entities appear. Each one becomes a class with a single responsibility.

metadata.alt: The core entities and how they connect

items: VendingMachine: the context that owns the balance, the current state, and coordinates everything
State: an interface with one implementation per machine mode, IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispenseState
Item: a product with a code, a name, and a price in cents
ItemShelf: one slot holding a quantity of a single item
Inventory: the map of shelf codes to shelves
Coin: an enum of accepted denominations, each carrying its value in cents
ChangeDispenser: tracks the coin float and makes change
PaymentStrategy: an interface for how money is collected, cash today, card tomorrow

blocks.text: Notice what is deliberately absent: there is no Display or Logger entity in the core. Presentation concerns attach from outside through events, keeping the core model pure.
Naming the relationship types shows the interviewer you know the difference between owning, holding, and pointing at another object.

metadata.alt: Composition, aggregation, association, and inheritance in this design

items: VendingMachine composes Inventory and ChangeDispenser: they are created with the machine and die with it
Inventory composes its ItemShelf objects: a shelf has no meaning outside its inventory
ItemShelf aggregates an Item: the product definition exists independently and could be shared by shelves
VendingMachine aggregates a PaymentStrategy: strategies are created outside and swapped freely
VendingMachine holds a reference to its current State and delegates every action to it
States call back into the machine to read balance, reach the inventory, and switch states
IdleState, HasMoneyState, and DispenseState implement the State interface
CashPayment and CardPayment implement the PaymentStrategy interface

blocks.text: The class diagram below captures the whole design in one view: the machine composes inventory and change handling, delegates behaviour to the State hierarchy, and holds a swappable payment strategy.

metadata.alt: UML class diagram of the vending machine

blocks.text: Reading guide: solid diamond arrows are composition, open diamonds are aggregation, dashed triangle arrows are interface realisation, and the plain arrow from VendingMachine to State is the delegation that powers the State pattern.
8.1 What to say while drawing this
blocks.content: 8.1 What to say while drawing this

blocks.text: Start from VendingMachine, then say: the machine never contains behaviour branching, it forwards every call to its current State. Then sketch the three states, the inventory chain, and finish with the strategy interface for payments.
The parts below take this one piece at a time, beginning with State Pattern (the backbone).
Why needed: the same user action means different things depending on what has already happened. Pressing A1 while idle must be rejected; pressing A1 after inserting money starts a purchase.

Why it is the best choice: the alternative is boolean flags checked in every method, which grows combinatorially and hides the legal transitions. With State, each mode is one small class and the transition graph is explicit.
What it solves: it eliminates scattered conditionals, makes illegal actions impossible to forget, and turns adding a new mode into adding one class.

metadata.alt: State transitions: Idle, HasMoney, and Dispense

blocks.text: Why needed: cash is only the first payment method. Cards, wallets, and QR payments will come.
Why it is the best choice: payment is a swappable algorithm chosen per transaction, which is exactly what Strategy models. Inheritance on the machine would freeze one payment type into the hierarchy.
What it solves: new payment types are new classes; the machine and states never change, honouring the Open Closed Principle.
Why needed: one physical machine maps naturally to one machine object, and hardware access must not be duplicated.

Why acceptable here: a lazily initialised, thread safe singleton is fine for the demo, but flag the tradeoff: singletons complicate testing, so in production prefer dependency injection with a single instance.
Why needed: screens, receipt printers, and monitoring all react to machine events. What it solves: the states publish events without knowing who listens, keeping presentation out of the core.
Name a pattern only with its justification. State because behaviour changes by mode, Strategy because payment is a swappable algorithm.
blocks.content: Name a pattern only with its justification. State because behaviour changes by mode, Strategy because payment is a swappable algorithm.

blocks.text: For each class: its single responsibility, its attributes, and its methods.

items: Responsibility: own the transaction context and delegate every action to the current state
Attributes: state, inventory, changeDispenser, balance in cents, selectedCode
Methods: insertMoney(coin), selectItem(code), dispense(), refund(), setState(state), plus operator methods restock and refillCoins
IdleState responsibility: accept the first money and move to HasMoney; reject everything else
HasMoneyState responsibility: accumulate money, validate selections, allow refund
DispenseState responsibility: release the item, return change, reset to Idle
Attributes: none, states are stateless and reusable; all data lives on the machine
Responsibility: immutable product definition
Attributes: code, name, priceInCents
Methods: getters only, no behaviour
Responsibility: guard the stock count of one product
Attributes: code, item, quantity
Methods: isAvailable(), tryDispense() which atomically checks and decrements, addStock(count)
Responsibility: constant time lookup from shelf code to shelf
Attributes: a HashMap of code to ItemShelf
Methods: addShelf(code, item, qty), getShelf(code)
Responsibility: track the coin float and make exact change
Attributes: a Map of Coin to count
Methods: add(coin, count), canMakeChange(amount), makeChange(amount)
Coin: PENNY(1), NICKEL(5), DIME(10), QUARTER(25), ONE(100), FIVE(500), each holding its value
PaymentStrategy: pay(amount) returning success; CashPayment and CardPayment implement it

blocks.text: Two interfaces carry the whole design, and both exist for the same reason: the machine must depend on a stable abstraction while the concrete behaviour varies.

metadata.alt: The two interfaces and their implementations

blocks.text: Why State is an interface: the machine must be able to hold any mode through one type. Every state answers the same four actions, even when the answer is a rejection, so no caller ever needs to know which mode is active.

Why PaymentStrategy is an interface: the machine needs money collected, not a particular way of collecting it. Depending on the abstraction inverts the dependency and lets payment tech evolve independently.
Program to an interface, not an implementation. The machine talks to State and PaymentStrategy, never to a concrete class.
blocks.content: Program to an interface, not an implementation. The machine talks to State and PaymentStrategy, never to a concrete class.

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a successful purchase with change

blocks.text: The user inserts two coins, selects A1, and the HasMoney state validates against the inventory and the change dispenser before switching to Dispense. Dispense releases the item, returns change, and resets to Idle.
12.2 Failure path: insufficient balance and refund
blocks.content: 12.2 Failure path: insufficient balance and refund

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a rejected selection followed by a refund

blocks.text: With only 25 cents in, the selection is rejected with a clear exception and the state does not change. The user cancels, the machine refunds the full balance and returns to Idle. Money is never lost on a failure.
Cancelling is always safe. Whatever has been inserted is returned in full through the change dispenser, the machine resets, and the state returns to Idle.

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a cancel: full refund and reset to Idle
The purchase flow with its validation gate

items: Machine is Idle; user inserts a coin; balance becomes visible and state moves to HasMoney
User inserts more coins; balance accumulates in HasMoney
User selects a code; the state checks the shelf exists, has stock, the balance covers the price, and change is possible
All checks pass; the machine records the selection and moves to Dispense
Dispense releases one unit from the shelf, computes change as balance minus price, and pays it out
The machine resets balance and selection and returns to Idle
Insufficient balance: selection throws, state stays HasMoney, user may add money or refund
Out of stock: selection throws, state stays HasMoney, other codes remain selectable
Cannot make change: selection is refused before dispensing, protecting the customer
Cancel mid transaction: refund returns the full balance and resets to Idle
Illegal action: the current state rejects it with a message, no crash, no corruption

items: insertMoney: legal in Idle and HasMoney, rejected during Dispense
selectItem: legal only in HasMoney; performs all validation before any state change
dispense: legal only in Dispense; the only method that mutates stock
refund: legal in HasMoney and Dispense; always returns exactly the current balance

blocks.text: Errors are part of the contract. Each failure category gets a specific, descriptive exception so callers can react precisely.

metadata.alt: The failure categories and their exceptions

items: Unknown shelf code: InvalidSelectionException with the offending code
Null or unaccepted denomination: rejected at the enum boundary, impossible by construction
Out of stock: OutOfStockException, state unchanged, balance untouched
Change unavailable: ChangeUnavailableException raised before dispensing, sale refused
Insufficient balance: InsufficientBalanceException carrying price and current balance
Action illegal in the current state: IllegalStateException from the state that rejected it
Dispense hardware failure: the transaction is rolled back and the balance refunded
Every exception leaves the machine in a consistent state; money is refunded or preserved, never lost

blocks.text: A good error is specific, leaves the machine consistent, and never eats the customer money.
blocks.content: A good error is specific, leaves the machine consistent, and never eats the customer money.

metadata.alt: Two buyers racing for the last item: the atomic check decides one winner

blocks.text: The classic race is two requests reading quantity 1 on the same shelf and both dispensing, driving stock to minus one. This is a check then act race and it must be closed.

items: The availability check and the decrement must be one atomic operation per shelf
Balance mutations within a transaction must be confined to one session thread
The coin float updates during change making must be atomic with the change computation

blocks.text: Lock at the smallest scope, the individual shelf, so different shelves never contend. An AtomicInteger with a compare and swap loop is an equivalent lock free alternative. Locking the whole machine would be correct but would serialise everything needlessly.
The test of the design is what happens when requirements change. Each common extension lands as new code, not edits.

metadata.alt: Extensions plug into existing abstractions without edits

items: New payment method: one new PaymentStrategy class; nothing else changes
New machine mode such as Maintenance or OutOfService: one new State class plus its transitions
New denomination: one new enum constant; change making adapts automatically
New product: pure data, a new shelf in the inventory, zero code
Discounts: decorate the price lookup before the balance check, states untouched
Display and telemetry: observers subscribing to machine events
Multi item carts: extend the selection to a list and validate the total
Remote inventory monitoring: publish stock events to a backend
Dynamic pricing: swap a PricingStrategy alongside the PaymentStrategy

metadata.alt: How the design maps to SOLID

items: Single Responsibility: Item holds data, ItemShelf guards stock, Inventory maps codes, ChangeDispenser owns money mechanics, each State owns one mode, the machine only coordinates
Open Closed: new payments, states, and denominations are added as new classes or constants without touching tested code
Liskov Substitution: any State implementation can stand wherever State is expected; the machine cannot tell them apart and never needs to
Interface Segregation: State has exactly the four actions a mode must answer; PaymentStrategy has one method; no fat interfaces forcing empty implementations
Dependency Inversion: the machine depends on the State and PaymentStrategy abstractions; concrete classes depend on those abstractions too, so the arrows of dependency point at interfaces

blocks.text: These are outcomes of the structure, not decorations. Because responsibilities are small and the machine talks to interfaces, SOLID falls out naturally.

metadata.alt: The edge cases the design must survive

items: Exact payment: change is zero, the dispenser pays nothing, and the flow completes normally
Overpayment with an empty float: detected by canMakeChange before sale, refused and refunded
Selecting the same code twice: the second select is rejected because the state is already Dispense
Refund with zero balance: Idle rejects it with nothing to refund
Restocking while a buyer is mid transaction: shelf locks keep counts consistent
Machine restarted mid transaction: with in memory state the balance is lost, which is why persistence of open transactions is listed as a production concern
A coin inserted during dispensing: rejected by DispenseState, returned to the user
Price of zero or negative: forbidden at construction time by validation in Item

blocks.text: The parts below take this one piece at a time, beginning with Time complexity.

items: insertMoney: O(1), an integer addition
selectItem: O(1) shelf lookup plus O(k) change feasibility over k denominations, k is 6, effectively constant
dispense: O(1) decrement plus O(c) coins of change, bounded by the amount over the smallest coin
restock and refillCoins: O(1) map updates
O(S) for S shelves in the inventory
O(k) for the coin float over k denominations
O(1) per transaction, only a balance and a selected code

blocks.text: Nothing grows with the number of transactions, and no operation scans the catalogue, so the machine stays constant time regardless of how large the product range gets.
The interview design is in memory, but a production machine persists its catalogue, stock, float, and sales. A minimal relational schema:

metadata.alt: Entity relationship diagram for persistent vending machine data

items: ITEM: the product catalogue, keyed by code
SHELF: current stock per shelf, foreign key to the item
TRANSACTION: one row per attempted sale with amount, change, and status for auditing
COIN_FLOAT: current count per denomination, updated atomically with each sale
Primary keys on code and txn_id cover point lookups
An index on TRANSACTION(created_at) supports daily reconciliation queries
An index on TRANSACTION(item_code) supports per product sales reporting

blocks.text: Writes should be transactional: decrement stock, update the float, and insert the transaction row in one unit so a crash never leaves them inconsistent.
The parts below take this one piece at a time, beginning with Possible optimizations.

items: Replace greedy change with bounded dynamic programming when the float runs low, so change is found whenever it exists
Precompute change feasibility per price point and invalidate on float changes
Use lock free atomics on shelves if contention ever matters
How would you add a maintenance mode? One new State that rejects buyer actions
State versus Strategy: State transitions itself over a lifecycle, Strategy is chosen from outside and stays fixed
How do you test this? Each state in isolation, transitions as a table of action and expected state, change making as pure functions
A fleet of machines reports stock and faults to a central service; the machine keeps working offline and syncs when connected
Central service stores per machine inventory keyed by machine id; the on device design remains exactly this one
Idempotent transaction upload prevents double counting sales on retries

blocks.text: The parts below take this one piece at a time, beginning with State classes versus an enum switch.
26.1 State classes versus an enum switch
blocks.content: 26.1 State classes versus an enum switch

blocks.text: A single enum with a switch per action is fewer files and fine for three states. It centralises transitions but reintroduces branching in every method and grows painful as modes multiply. Classes win once behaviour per mode is non trivial.

We keep states stateless and create them on transition. Alternatively, share singleton instances of each state to avoid allocation. Both are correct; singletons of states pair well with an enum based registry.

Greedy is simple and optimal for standard denominations but can fail with a constrained float. Bounded DP always finds change when it exists at a small compute cost. Ship greedy with a DP fallback when the float is low.
26.4 Machine level lock versus shelf level lock
blocks.content: 26.4 Machine level lock versus shelf level lock

blocks.text: One global lock is trivially correct but serialises everything. Per shelf locks add a little care for a lot of concurrency. For a fleet backend this choice matters far more than on one machine.
Exceptions keep the happy path clean and are idiomatic Java. Result objects make failures explicit in signatures. In an interview, exceptions with specific types communicate intent fastest.

items: Hardware confirmation: complete a sale only when the drop sensor confirms the item fell; otherwise auto refund
Crash safety: persist open transactions so a reboot can resume or refund; never strand customer money
Auditability: log every money movement with a transaction id for reconciliation
Telemetry: publish stock levels, float levels, and faults so operators restock before sellouts
Security: tamper detection on the cash box, signed firmware, and authenticated operator access
Observability: counters for sales, rejections by reason, and change failures reveal issues early
Testing: table driven state transition tests, property tests on change making, and a soak test for the shelf race
Idempotency: card charges carry an idempotency key so retries never double charge

blocks.text: Find the states, draw the transitions, program to interfaces, and give every responsibility its own small class. That is the whole game.
